newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech parties to discuss energy prices, rent hike.
newsitem.headline: Czech parties to discuss energy prices, rent hike.

text.p: Czech government parties meet on Thursday to discuss loosening controls on prices for energy and housing in a move which analysts say could boost inflation but help dampen high demand for consumer goods.
The three parties in the minority coalition are due to discuss at a conference a variety of proposals for further deregulation of household gas and electricity prices and rents.
"We would like to speed the process of increasing the prices to the real cost level this year," Deputy Finance Minister Jana Fuerstova told Reuters.
Deregulation is one of the most sensitive political issues in the Czech Republic, where many live in apartments with fixed low rents and with energy bills subsidised by industrial users.

But freeing prices is also seen as one of the key remaining items of unfinished business in Prague's transition to a market economy and some economists say much of Czechs' disposable income is translated into demand for, often imported, goods.

"The biggest problem as many economists and the government understand it is that there is a big over-hang of private demand which is not met from domestic sources," said analyst Jindrich Weiss of Zivnostenska Banka.
"There is a growing imbalance in foreign trade and in this situation it would be good at least to start to slow the long-term imbalance in regulated prices," he said.

Fuerstova said the ministry, headed by Finance Minister Ivan Kocarnik of the Civic Democratic Party (ODS) senior coalition partner, would propose a 35 percent increase in domestic electricity and gas prices from July 1 and a national average rent increase of 50 percent.
"It is a waste of electricity and gas by the residential sector. Because prices are so low, consumption is increasing every year very rapidly," she said.

The energy price increase would include a rise in value added tax to 22 percent for five percent, a move which the deputy minister said would bring half the revenue of the price increase to state budget coffers.

She said the proposed rent rise should bring more apartments on to the market. Some economists say unwillingness to move from low-rent flats is a key factor in the tightness of the labour market, a major sticking point in the Czech economic transformation.

The ODS, led by Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus, is generally seen as more cautious on deregulation than its junior partners, the conservative Civic Democratic Alliance and the centrist Christian Democrats (KDU-CSL), which have their own proposals.
The Trade and Industry Ministry, headed by Minister Vladimir Dlouhy of the ODA, also supports a 35 percent increase in domestic energy prices but not the VAT increase.
It wants the price increase to go to meet investment needs at power generation and distribution companies.
The central bank has cautioned against excessive rises in regulated prices, saying this could fuel inflation.
Fuerstova said the proposed price increases would boost inflation, which was 8.8 percent last year, by one percentage point. "The demand for other goods will decrease," she said.

Trade ministry energy department official Pavel Brychta said his ministry's proposals would raise inflation by three to four percentage points this year to a maximum 12 percent. He saw only a small impact on domestic demand.
Zivnostenska's Weiss said the price rises would raise this year's reported inflation but could ultimately reduce it.
"If the price hike would be quite high, it might push down spending on other goods and services and it might push down core inflation," he said.
